title: Renewables in Electricity Markets
text:
At the Technical University of Denmark, I developed and taught for many years an M.Sc. course on Renewables in Electricity Markets. All the course material is shared here for anyone who wants to learn about the topic. It covers the basics of electricity markets (day-ahead and balancing markets, ancillary services), the impact of renewables on markets, how renewable energy producers participate in electricity markets, and renewable energy analytics, mainly forecasting.
The course is built from ten modules of video lectures with slides. Six exercise sessions let you apply the ideas, and interviews with industry guests and former students show why it matters in practice.

title: Renewables in Electricity Markets
text:
Why renewables in electricity markets?
The topic sits where three of the major trends in electric energy systems over the last 10 to 20 years meet: the large-scale deployment of renewable energy generation, the deregulation of the electric power sector, and digitization. Together they have brought a wealth of challenges and opportunities, as two industry guests explain.


Olivier Corradi (Tomorrow) wants consumers to appraise the climate impact of their daily choices.



Christophe Lephilibert (GetBarry) is changing the way we relate to electricity consumption.

title: Joining inCommodities as Principal
text: As of 1 October 2026, I have joined inCommodities as Principal, while continuing as Professor at Imperial College London, Dyson School of Design Engineering.

title: About
text:
I am a Principal at inCommodities, a data-driven energy trading company, and a Professor at Imperial College London, Dyson School of Design Engineering. I am an IEEE Fellow (class of 2020), an INFORMS member and an IIF director, and I was on the Clarivate Highly Cited Researchers list in 2019, 2020 and 2021 (cross-field) for work in statistics, meteorology, economics and power and energy engineering.
Before Imperial, I was a Professor at the Technical University of Denmark, first in the Department of Electrical Engineering and then in the Department of Technology, Management and Economics. I have been a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford (Mathematical Institute) and the University of Washington (Department of Statistics), and spent a year at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) working on ensemble forecasting of surface winds. I have also been a visiting professor at École Normale Supérieure de Rennes, and a Simons Fellow at the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences in Cambridge for the Mathematics of Energy Systems programme.
What has interested me most over the last decades is how to generate optimal value from data, for society and for the various stakeholders involved. I have mainly worked on energy and meteorology, as well as shipping, logistics and business analytics. That brings together data science, analytics, operations research and management science, game theory and mechanism design. Some of the work I am known for includes probabilistic forecasting and forecast verification, peer-to-peer and community-based electricity markets, coordination of energy markets, and collaborative and market-based analytics such as data and analytics markets.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
The International Journal of Forecasting (IJF) is the leading journal in its field. It is the official publication of the International Institute of Forecasters (IIF) and shares its aims and scope: to unify the field and bridge the gap between theory and practice, making forecasting useful and relevant for decision and policy makers. The journal places strong emphasis on empirical studies, evaluation, implementation research and ways of improving forecasting practice, and is open to many points of view. Reviewing is double-blind.
I wrote an editorial in early 2020 when I became Editor-in-Chief.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
Topics covered
Economic and econometric forecasting, marketing, new products, finance, production, technology, business, government and the military, demographics, energy, climate, crime, seasonal adjustment, time series, legal and political aspects, implementation, judgmental and psychological aspects, the impact of forecast uncertainty on decision making, organizational aspects, sport, machine learning, forecasting methodology, elections, and big data.
The journal publishes research papers, research notes, discussion articles, book reviews, editorials and letters. Data and code associated with published articles are provided as online supplements on ScienceDirect.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
Submitting a paper
The IJF welcomes submissions relevant to the science and practice of forecasting: methodological and applied papers, new datasets and forecasting competitions, short communications, book reviews and interviews.
Submit an article

Preferred keywords
Online supplements. For empirical studies, the description of the method and data should allow replication. Please submit code and data to be published as an online supplement. Appendices with additional results can be supplements too.
LaTeX is encouraged. Use the Elsevier elsarticle class, submit a PDF, and use BibTeX or BibLaTeX. Save figures as PDF or EPS, not JPG or WMF. After acceptance we will ask for the source files.
Word files are also accepted. Save equations as equation objects rather than images, use high-resolution figures, and use the APA style if you manage references with EndNote.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
The International Journal of Forecasting (IJF) is the leading journal in its field. It is the official publication of the International Institute of Forecasters (IIF) and shares its aims and scope: to unify the field and bridge the gap between theory and practice, making forecasting useful and relevant for decision and policy makers. The journal places strong emphasis on empirical studies, evaluation, implementation research and ways of improving forecasting practice, and is open to many points of view. Reviewing is double-blind.
I wrote an editorial in early 2020 when I became Editor-in-Chief.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
Topics covered
Economic and econometric forecasting, marketing, new products, finance, production, technology, business, government and the military, demographics, energy, climate, crime, seasonal adjustment, time series, legal and political aspects, implementation, judgmental and psychological aspects, the impact of forecast uncertainty on decision making, organizational aspects, sport, machine learning, forecasting methodology, elections, and big data.
The journal publishes research papers, research notes, discussion articles, book reviews, editorials and letters. Data and code associated with published articles are provided as online supplements on ScienceDirect.

title: About
text:
I am a Principal at inCommodities, a data-driven energy trading company, and a Professor at Imperial College London, Dyson School of Design Engineering. I am an IEEE Fellow (class of 2020), an INFORMS member and an IIF director, and I was on the Clarivate Highly Cited Researchers list in 2019, 2020 and 2021 (cross-field) for work in statistics, meteorology, economics and power and energy engineering.
Before Imperial, I was a Professor at the Technical University of Denmark, first in the Department of Electrical Engineering and then in the Department of Technology, Management and Economics. I have been a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford (Mathematical Institute) and the University of Washington (Department of Statistics), and spent a year at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) working on ensemble forecasting of surface winds. I have also been a visiting professor at École Normale Supérieure de Rennes, and a Simons Fellow at the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences in Cambridge for the Mathematics of Energy Systems programme.
What has interested me most over the last decades is how to generate optimal value from data, for society and for the various stakeholders involved. I have mainly worked on energy and meteorology, as well as shipping, logistics and business analytics. That brings together data science, analytics, operations research and management science, game theory and mechanism design. Some of the work I am known for includes probabilistic forecasting and forecast verification, peer-to-peer and community-based electricity markets, coordination of energy markets, and collaborative and market-based analytics such as data and analytics markets.

title: Renewables in Electricity Markets
text:
At the Technical University of Denmark, I developed and taught for many years an M.Sc. course on Renewables in Electricity Markets. All the course material is shared here for anyone who wants to learn about the topic. It covers the basics of electricity markets (day-ahead and balancing markets, ancillary services), the impact of renewables on markets, how renewable energy producers participate in electricity markets, and renewable energy analytics, mainly forecasting.
The course is built from ten modules of video lectures with slides. Six exercise sessions let you apply the ideas, and interviews with industry guests and former students show why it matters in practice.

title: Renewables in Electricity Markets
text:
Why renewables in electricity markets?
The topic sits where three of the major trends in electric energy systems over the last 10 to 20 years meet: the large-scale deployment of renewable energy generation, the deregulation of the electric power sector, and digitization. Together they have brought a wealth of challenges and opportunities, as two industry guests explain.


Olivier Corradi (Tomorrow) wants consumers to appraise the climate impact of their daily choices.



Christophe Lephilibert (GetBarry) is changing the way we relate to electricity consumption.
